title: The $1.50 Hot Dog Costco Won't Raise

scenes.narration: In {2013,|twenty thirteen,} Costco's CEO went to the co-founder with bad news. Jim, we can't sell this hot dog for a buck fifty. We are losing our rear ends.
The co-founder's answer: if you raise the effing hot dog, I will kill you. Figure it out.

data.quote: If you raise the [effing] hot dog, I will kill you. *Figure it out.*
data.note: as recalled by CEO Craig Jelinek (425 Business, 2018)

scenes.narration: So they figured it out. Forty years later, a hot dog and a soda still cost {$1.50.|a dollar fifty.}
Because the hot dog was never the product. The real product makes Costco over five billion dollars a year, and there's a good chance it's in your wallet right now.

lines.text: The hot dog isn't the product
The *real* one is in your wallet

scenes.narration: Last year alone, Costco sold {245.1 million|two hundred forty-five million} of these combos. So let's follow the money: what one costs, what it earns, and what it's really for.

data.label: hot dog combos sold
data.source: Source: Costco annual shareholder meeting, Jan 2026

scenes.narration: Part one. The price that should be {$4.50.|four fifty.}
Since {1985,|nineteen eighty-five,} gas, rent and groceries all got more expensive. The hot dog didn't move.
If the combo had simply kept up with inflation since {1985,|nineteen eighty-five,} it would cost about {$4.50|four dollars and fifty cents} today.
Meanwhile, the hot dog, the bun and the soda are estimated to cost Costco around a dollar.

data.title: What Costco keeps per combo
data.source: Cost estimate: The Motley Fool, Dec 2025

scenes.narration: Add staff, space and equipment, and what's left is pennies. One employee claimed it's about eight cents a combo.
So how did they figure it out? They switched sodas to save money, and they built their own hot dog factories.
If you like seeing the receipts behind everyday prices, subscribe. There's a new one every week.
Part two. The real product.
To shop at Costco, you need a membership. In the United States, a basic card costs {$65|sixty-five dollars} a year. The executive tier costs {$130.|a hundred and thirty.}
At the end of fiscal {2025,|twenty twenty-five,} Costco had {81 million|eighty-one million} paid members.
Remember that five billion? Here it is: membership fees brought in {$5.3 billion|five point three billion dollars} in a single year.
Now put that next to Costco's total profit for the same year: about {$8.1 billion.|eight point one billion dollars.}
In other words, membership fees alone equal roughly two thirds of everything Costco earns.

data.title: Membership fees as a share of net income

scenes.narration: Everything else, the groceries, the TVs, the tires, and yes, the hot dogs, is priced so close to cost that the shopping itself barely pays.
Costco caps most markups at around fourteen to fifteen percent. The goal isn't profit on each item. It's a reason to come back.

data.label: The goal: a reason to *come back*

scenes.narration: Part three. Why the hot dog has to stay at {$1.50.|a dollar fifty.}
A membership only works if members feel they're getting a deal, every single visit.

lines.text: every visit must *feel* like a deal

scenes.narration: The hot dog is the deal you can taste. It's often the last thing you see on the way out. It's advertising that customers pay for, two hundred forty-five million times a year.
And it's not just the hot dog. Costco's rotisserie chicken has cost {$4.99|four ninety-nine} since {2009.|two thousand nine.}
To keep it there, Costco built its own chicken operation in Nebraska, designed to produce more than two million chickens a week at full capacity.

data.kicker: Chickens per week at full capacity
data.label: Costco's own operation in *Nebraska*

scenes.narration: And members keep coming back. In the US and Canada, {92.3%|ninety-two point three percent} of members renewed. Worldwide, it was {89.8%.|eighty-nine point eight percent.}
Every renewal is almost pure profit. Costco doesn't have to sell you anything extra to collect it.
So when the co-founder said he'd kill anyone who raised the price, he wasn't protecting a hot dog.

He was protecting five billion dollars a year. Costco doesn't mainly make money selling you things. It makes money because you pay for the right to buy them. Next week: why movie theater popcorn costs what it does.

summary: Costco's CEO said the $1.50 hot dog was losing money. The co-founder said: raise it and I'll kill you. Here's why: the hot dog was never the product.

hooks.hook: In 2013, Costco's CEO went to the co-founder with bad news: we can't sell this hot dog for a buck fifty. The answer: raise it and I will kill you.
In 1985 a hot dog and a soda at Costco cost $1.50. Forty years later, it still costs $1.50.
Costco sold 245 million hot dogs in a single year, and made almost nothing on them. On purpose.
Why hasn't Costco's hot dog changed price in forty years, when everything else has?
Costco's $1.50 hot dog isn't a bargain. It's the most important ad in the store.
The most important number in Costco's annual report isn't the price of anything it sells.
